paper_title: GeoState: Learning View-Decoupled Geometry States for 3D World Modeling

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent 3D world models increasingly use features from geometry foundation models (GFMs) as predictive world states, benefiting from their rich geometric priors. However, the view dependence of these features entangles scene dynamics with camera-induced variation, making the resulting state evolution harder to predict. We propose GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry representation for predictive 3D world modeling that separates scene-state evolution from camera-dependent observation. Specifically, a scene tokenizer aggregates multi-view GFM features into a view-decoupled scene state, which a geometry decoder queries using camera rays. An autoregressive world model then predicts future scene states, while camera motion is modeled separately. The predicted states can therefore be decoded under either predicted or externally specified cameras, while retaining a single context-derived scale throughout the rollout without per-frame scale alignment. Experiments show that GeoState outperforms prior 3D world models on Waymo, supports geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and generalizes zero-shot to KITTI and nuScenes. Project page: https://hongchang-liu.github.io/GeoState-project-page/

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Learning to predict how the physical world evolves is central goal of world modeling (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018), with direct relevance to autonomous driving, robotics, and embodied intelligence. Visual world models predict the future in pixel space (Hu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024b; Gao et al., 2024; NVIDIA et al., 2025), which can introduce substantial representational redundancy and make geometric consistency difficult to maintain. This has motivated increasing interest in 3D world models, which represent and predict future environments in geometrically grounded state spaces. By explicitly encoding spatial structure and 3D relationships, these representations provide structured and geometrically grounded state space that more directly reflects the real world. Recent 3D world models have explored range of structured geometric state spaces, including depth, occupancy, point-based representations, and 3D Gaussians (Zheng et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Zuo et al., 2025). In parallel, geometry foundation models (GFMs) have substantially advanced feed-forward 3D perception by learning rich geometric representations directly from RGB observations (Wang et al., 2024a; Yang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b;a; 2026). Benefiting from large-scale pretraining, these representations capture strong geometric priors that generalize across scenes and tasks, making them attractive state spaces for predictive world modeling. Building on this capability, recent approaches have begun to directly model temporal evolution in pretrained geometry feature spaces (Sun et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). In particular, VGGT-World (Sun et al., 2026) treats frozen VGGT features as world states and predicts their future evolution, demonstrating the potential of GFM representations for 3D forecasting. Despite the strong performance achieved by recent GFM-based 3D world models, strong representation for geometric perception is not necessarily an appropriate state representation for world

GFM features are typically constructed from and organized around the observing views, so changes in camera viewpoint can induce substantial changes in the representation even when the underlying physical scene remains unchanged. When such features are directly used as predictive states, temporal model would account simultaneously for genuine scene evolution and camerainduced variation, although these arise from fundamentally different sources. In particular, even static scene can undergo substantial changes in feature space as the camera moves, forcing the temporal model to predict viewpoint-dependent transformations that do not correspond to physical scene evolution. This unnecessary variation makes the latent dynamics more complex and therefore harder to predict over long horizons. FR3D (Morbitzer et al., 2026) also shows that separating egomotion from scene forecasting can improve temporal modeling, but its predictive state still inherits the view-dependent structure of the underlying reconstruction representation. We argue that such separation should instead be built into the representation itself: the state should describe what the world is, while the camera should determine only how that world is observed. To this end, we introduce GeoState, view-decoupled geometry state learned from pretrained GFM features. Given multi-view observations, scene tokenizer compresses their geometry features into compact scene state represented in shared scene coordinate system, while the query viewpoint is introduced only during decoding. Specifically, geometry decoder takes the scene state together with rays from query camera and predicts the geometry observed from that viewpoint. Consequently, the same scene state can be queried repeatedly from different viewpoints without re-encoding the scene. This transforms view-conditioned GFM features into representation in which scene geometry is explicitly separated from camera-dependent observation. Building on this representation, we formulate 3D world modeling directly in the scene-state space. The temporal model can therefore focus solely on predicting scene dynamics, while camera evolution is modeled independently. At inference time, predicted future state can be decoded using either separately predicted camera trajectory or user-controlled camera. Our formulation also maintains consistent scene gauge throughout temporal prediction and geometry decoding, avoiding the need for per-frame scale alignment during rollout. We evaluate our approach on large-scale dynamic driving scenes, using Waymo (Sun et al., 2020) for in-domain evaluation and KITTI (Geiger et al., 2012) and nuScenes (Caesar et al., 2020) for zeroshot transfer. Our approach outperforms the compared world models in depth forecasting across all reported horizons, while maintaining consistent scale throughout the forecasting rollout. Experiments further demonstrate geometrically consistent querying across viewpoints and generalization across driving datasets. Ablation results show that view decoupling makes the scene representation more predictable. Together, these findings support view-decoupled geometry states derived from pretrained GFMs as an effective representation for predictive 3D world modeling. Our contributions are threefold: We identify viewpoint coupling in geometry foundation model features as limitation when using them as predictive world states, and introduce GeoState, view-decoupled geometry state derived from pretrained GFM representations that separates scene content from how the scene is observed. We develop scene-state learning framework that realizes GeoState through Scene Tokenizer that aggregates multi-view GFM features into shared scene state and queryconditioned Geometry Decoder that introduces the query viewpoint only at decoding time. We formulate 3D world model that predicts scene evolution directly in GeoState space while modeling camera evolution separately, and demonstrate long-horizon geometry forecasting, geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and zero-shot generalization across driving datasets without per-frame scale alignment.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: 2.1 3D WORLD MODELS Recent world models increasingly move beyond pixel-space prediction toward structured 3D scene modeling and forecasting. Copilot4D (Zhang et al., 2024) and ViDAR (Yang et al., 2024) forecast future point clouds, while OccWorld (Zheng et al., 2024) and DOME (Gu et al., 2024) predict scene

DIO (Diehl et al., 2025) represents future scene geometry and motion through decomposable implicit occupancy-flow fields, and GaussianWorld (Zuo et al., 2025) models scene evolution in 3D Gaussian space for streaming occupancy prediction. More recently, several approaches directly use learned geometry representations as predictive world states. VGGT-World (Sun et al., 2026) forecasts future VGGT features, while GeoWAM (Lu et al., 2026) learns geometry-aware predictive states for autonomous driving. FR3D (Morbitzer et al., 2026) predicts the latent state of pretrained 3D reconstruction model while modeling ego-motion separately. In contrast, we remove viewpoint dependence from the geometry state itself and introduce viewpoint only as query condition during decoding.

sections.title: 2.2 GEOMETRY FOUNDATION MODELS
sections.content: Geometry foundation models provide strong pretrained priors for multi-view 3D perception. DUSt3R (Wang et al., 2024a) formulates reconstruction through pointmap prediction, while Fast3R (Yang et al., 2025) scales joint reconstruction to larger collections of views. CUT3R (Wang et al., 2025b) introduces persistent latent state for continuously integrating observations, and VGGT (Wang et al., 2025a) unifies camera estimation, depth, point maps, and tracking in feedforward architecture. VGGT-Ω (Wang et al., 2026) further strengthens this paradigm for dynamic 3D scenes, making it natural geometry backbone for our setting. We build on its pretrained geometric features and reformulate them into compact, view-decoupled scene-level representation better suited for temporal world modeling. 2.3 COMPACT 3D REPRESENTATIONS related line of work compresses multi-view observations into compact scene representations. LVSM (Jin et al., 2025) encodes input views into fixed-length set of latent tokens for novelview synthesis, while Surflo (Guedon et al., 2026) aggregates dense VGGT features into fixed-size global latent representation for efficient 3D surface reconstruction. 3DRAE (Wei et al., 2026) further learns fixed-length, view-decoupled 3D latent space that can be queried from arbitrary cameras. These works demonstrate that multi-view observations can be represented without retaining separate dense representation for each view. While they focus primarily on static scene reconstruction or novel-view synthesis, our work investigates whether such scene-level representations can serve as predictive states for temporal world modeling.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Datasets. We pretrain the Scene Tokenizer and ray-conditioned decoder on approximately 10k multi-view scenes from DL3DV (Ling et al., 2024), TartanAir (Wang et al., 2020), RealEstate10K (Zhou et al., 2018), CO3D (Reizenstein et al., 2021), and WildRGB-D (Xia et al., 2024), using ground-truth depth where available and VGGT-Ω (Wang et al., 2026) pseudo-depth otherwise. We then adapt both modules on subset of the Waymo Open Dataset (Sun et al., 2020) selected for static scene content. World Model training uses approximately 140k windows from 800 segments, each containing four context and seven future states at 0.2 intervals, with FRONT, FRONT LEFT, and FRONT RIGHT context views. We evaluate on 100 Waymo windows held out from model selection, 113 eligible KITTI (Geiger et al., 2012) drives, and all 150 scenes in the nuScenes (Caesar et al., 2020) validation split. Further dataset selection and sampling details are provided in Appendix A.5.

Without target-dataset adaptation, our model with predicted cameras outperforms DINO-Foresight, VGGT-World, and the reported FR3D results on both metrics across all reported horizons on both datasets. These results support that GeoState captures transferable geometric structure. Moreover, our predicted states consistently outperform camera-matched Copy-Last under both ground-truth and predicted cameras, showing that the learned scene dynamics also generalize beyond the training domain. 4.5 ABLATION STUDIES Geometric Reconstruction Quality. We first examine whether compressing GFM features into GeoState preserves their geometric information. Table 3 compares direct VGGT-Ω depth predictions with depth reconstructed through our Scene Tokenizer and Geometry Decoder using groundtruth query cameras. Both use target-time RGB observations and are evaluated against ground-truth LiDAR depth. Their comparable accuracy shows that the fixed-length GeoState preserves the geometric information required for accurate reconstruction, providing compact and geometrically faithful representation for subsequent world modeling. Effect of the View-Decoupled Scene State. We compare GeoState with feature-compression baseline that directly compresses VGGT-Ω features into 512 512 latent state. For fair comparison with the feature-compression baseline, only the target FRONT GFM output block is passed to the Scene Tokenizer. Both representations use the same world model, training data, forecasting objectives, optimization, and evaluation protocol; implementation details are provided in Appendix A.5.4. As shown in Table 4, the two representations achieve comparable reconstruction quality, but GeoState is substantially easier to predict, improving AbsRel and δ1 at every horizon. Because the two representations achieve comparable reconstruction quality, the forecasting gap is unlikely to arise from reconstruction accuracy. Instead, the results suggest that GeoState provides more predictable state space for temporal modeling. By separating scene content from viewpointdependent observation, GeoState reduces camera-induced variation in the state dynamics, allowing the World Model to focus more directly on the underlying evolution of scene geometry.

We ablate state supervision during one-step initialization and autoregressive rollout while retaining decoded-depth supervision in all settings. Table 5 shows that onestep state supervision consistently improves forecasting, providing useful target for initializing local state transitions. In contrast, extending latent matching throughout the rollout degrades longhorizon performance. These findings support using state matching to initialize local transitions while supervising autoregressive predictions through decoded geometry rather than enforcing unique latent trajectory.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented GeoState, view-decoupled geometry state learned from GFM features for predictive 3D world modeling. By separating scene evolution from camera-dependent observation, GeoState provides scene representation that can be predicted more effectively over time and queried from different viewpoints. Future work may extend this framework to embodied settings, where predictive scene states could support perception, planning, and interaction in dynamic environments.

Each training sample contains four observed poses at t0.6, t0.4, t0.2, and t, together with ten future poses at 0.2 intervals. The objective combines absolute pose error, adjacent relative-pose error, and ray-endpoint error with weights 1.0, 0.5, and 0.2, respectively. Rotation errors are converted to metric displacement using 10 lever arm. We first train for 12,000 steps with direct ten-horizon supervision using AdamW, batch size 1,024, weight decay 0.05, and cosine learning-rate schedule from 104 to 106 after 300 warm-up steps. We then continue for another 12,000 steps with closed-loop training, recursively applying the predictor over four consecutive rollout chunks. The closed-loop loss is weighted by 0.5. This phase uses batch size 384, 100-step warm-up, and cosine learning-rate schedule from 5 105 to 5 107. Gradients are clipped to norm 1.0 throughout motion training. Second, we train the visual adapter while keeping the motion backbone frozen. We use the same pose-based supervision, with the relative-pose and ray-endpoint terms both weighted by 0.5 and 20 rotation lever arm. A.4.1 WAYMO DATA CONSTRUCTION We use binary motion partition for Waymo. Motion labels are derived from the annotated 3D tracks of vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists over each eleven-state window (four observed and seven future states at 0.2 intervals). box observation must contain at least three LiDAR points and track must be observed in at least two states. We mark track as moving when its median speed exceeds 0.75 m/s for vehicle, 0.25 m/s for pedestrian, or 0.50 m/s for cyclist. window is Dynamic if it contains at least one such visible moving track and Static otherwise. This partition yields 114,735 Dynamic and 24,632 Static training windows. A.4.2 SCENE TOKENIZER AND DECODER TRAINING Multi-view pretraining uses 9,496 scenes, comprising 2,834 from DL3DV, 2,818 from TartanAir, 2,142 from RealEstate10K, 941 from CO3D, and 761 from WildRGB-D. To train the tokenizer with different visible-view configurations, anchor-view and random-view dropout each use probability 0.4 at the memory level. For each training sample with at least two source views, we apply one of three mutually exclusive memory-level operations: mask the anchor-view patch block with probability 0.4, mask one uniformly sampled non-anchor view block with probability 0.4, or retain all view blocks with probability 0.2. Single-view samples retain their only view.

For each training example, the frozen GFM jointly processes four historical timestamps and one target timestamp, with FRONT, FRONT LEFT, and FRONT RIGHT at each timestamp.
